The investigation, published in the journal Infectious Agents and Cancer, examined both clinical and community cohorts to gather baseline evidence on high-risk viral distribution and relevant socio-behavioural characteristics. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus constitutes the primary cause of cervical malignancies, yet precise regional data regarding viral prevalence, specific genotype circulation, and linked demographic factors have historically remained sparse across several areas of India. To evaluate these regional dynamics, the investigation recruited a total of 625 women between the ages of 30 and 60 years across two distinct healthcare delivery settings. Participant enrollment took place through a hospital-based gynaecology outpatient department alongside 11 community screening outreach camps operating within the Central Gujarat region. All 625 participants enrolled in the study underwent concurrent diagnostic evaluations comprising Liquid-Based Cytology and molecular testing via real-time polymerase chain reaction. The researchers conducted descriptive analyses to determine the frequency of high-risk viral infection and map genotype distribution across the cohort, alongside exploratory statistical assessments to examine how measured patient characteristics correlated with laboratory-confirmed viral positivity. Discover more Check Symptoms Book a Checkup Order DNA Kits genotypes Cancer Across the complete study population, molecular testing identified high-risk human papillomavirus infection in 20 of the 625 participating women, yielding the aggregate prevalence figure of 3.2 percent. When evaluated by recruitment source, viral positivity varied between the two examination cohorts: the hospital-based outpatient cohort demonstrated a high-risk prevalence rate of 4.29 percent, whereas the community-based outreach cohort recorded a lower positivity rate of 2.17 percent. Among the 20 women testing positive for high-risk strains, genotype distribution analysis revealed that HPV-18 was the predominant variant, detected in 50.0 percent (10 of 20) of cases. HPV-16 represented the second most common variant, observed in 35.0 percent (7 of 20) of positive specimens, while other high-risk genotypes collectively accounted for the remaining 15.0 percent (3 of 20). The investigators also conducted univariate exploratory analyses using crude odds ratios with 95 percent confidence intervals and Fisher’s exact tests to identify potential associations between participant characteristics and high-risk viral detection. These statistical comparisons indicated that reported tobacco chewing was strongly associated with high-risk viral positivity, presenting a crude odds ratio of 32.85 (95% CI 9.43–114.42; p < 0.001). Furthermore, parity of greater than two children was associated with higher viral detection (OR 3.03, 95% CI 1.18–7.77; p = 0.018), as was an age at marriage below 18 years (OR 3.50, 95% CI 1.33–9.20; p = 0.009) and a reported history of menstrual irregularity (OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.11–7.01; p = 0.012). A notable clinical observation emerged when comparing initial cervical cytology classifications with subsequent histological evaluations among high-risk virus-positive participants who underwent colposcopy-directed biopsy. In the cytology assessments, 90.0 percent of the virus-positive individuals were categorized as having negative or low-grade cellular findings. However, subsequent histopathological examination of biopsy tissue identified cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades II or III (CIN II/III) in 45.0 percent of these cases, while invasive cervical carcinoma was histologically confirmed in 15.0 percent, demonstrating that substantial underlying cervical tissue abnormalities may exist despite unremarkable or low-grade screening cytology. In detailing their conclusions, the authors emphasized that while the findings provide valuable preliminary epidemiological data for Central Gujarat, the results must be interpreted with caution. The study’s cross-sectional design precludes establishing temporal sequences or causal relationships, and the total number of confirmed high-risk viral cases was limited to 20 individuals. Consequently, the research team highlighted the necessity of conducting larger, multicentre investigations across India to validate genotype patterns, rigorously evaluate potential socio-behavioural risk factors, and inform regional cervical cancer screening protocols and public health prevention strategies. High-grade cervical lesions, designated as CIN2+, are critical precursors to cervical cancer. The clinical investigation specifically examined human papillomavirus infection, cervical cytology abnormalities, and vaccination status to determine their association with histopathologically confirmed disease. Conducted in an Iranian colposcopy population, the study reviewed medical records spanning a ten-year period, from January 2014 to January 2024. All 246 female participants had undergone colposcopic evaluation during this timeframe. The authors collected data on patient demographics, including age and marital status, alongside clinical characteristics, cervical cytology, human papillomavirus status, and documented HPV vaccination history. Biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ was defined as histopathologically diagnosed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, grade 3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or invasive cervical cancer. Viral testing utilized the PaxView® Kit to detect human papillomavirus and identify high-risk genotypes. To evaluate factors linked to CIN2+, investigators performed univariable and multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression analyses, reporting adjusted odds ratios and 95 percent confidence intervals. Discover more Find Skin Care Check Symptoms Infection infection Study Biology Of the 246 women analyzed in the retrospective study, 50 patients, or 20.3 percent, were diagnosed with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ lesions, while 196 women were categorized as CIN2−. Among the 50 women with CIN2+, 37 cases, or 74.0 percent, were classified as CIN2, and 10 cases, or 20.0 percent, were CIN3. Adenocarcinoma in situ was identified in 2 women, representing 4.0 percent, and invasive cervical cancer was diagnosed in 1 patient, representing 2.0 percent. The distribution of HPV status and cytological results differed significantly between women with CIN2+ and those without, with both differences yielding p-values of less than 0.001. HPV16/18 infection appeared in 56.0 percent of women with CIN2+ compared to 28.6 percent of those in the CIN2− group. In contrast, HPV-negative results were observed in 18.0 percent of the CIN2+ cohort versus 39.8 percent of CIN2− participants. Cytology showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, or HSIL, was recorded in 38.0 percent of CIN2+ cases compared with 10.7 percent of CIN2− cases. In addition, an absence of HPV vaccination was documented in 42.0 percent of the CIN2+ group versus 16.8 percent of women in the comparison group. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression demonstrated that three key factors were independently associated with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+. HPV16/18 infection yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 3.94, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.70 to 9.74 and a p-value of 0.001. Lack of HPV vaccination was associated with higher odds of CIN2+, showing an adjusted odds ratio of 2.20, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.03 to 4.65 and a p-value of 0.042. Women with HSIL cytology exhibited higher odds of CIN2+ than those with normal cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, designated as NILM, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.84, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.09 to 7.54 and a p-value of 0.031. Age, marital status, and other high-risk HPV genotypes showed no statistically significant independent association with CIN2+. The investigators noted that the observed association between the lack of HPV vaccination and higher odds of CIN2+ requires cautious interpretation by clinicians and researchers. Because vaccination timing relative to initial HPV exposure was not recorded in the retrospective dataset, the finding could reflect unmeasured confounding parameters. Prospective studies examining vaccination timing and pre-vaccination HPV status are required to clarify this relationship. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive systematic review synthesizing twelve longitudinal studies across eleven countries has revealed that the temporal stability of Lactobacillus-dominated microbial communities in the cervicovaginal tract is the most consistent microbiome feature associated with human papillomavirus clearance and the regression of cervical pre-cancerous lesions. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the investigation systematically examined how dynamic shifts across community state types correlate with viral persistence, viral clearance, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia transitions over time. Cervical cancer represents the fourth most common malignancy in women worldwide, responsible for an estimated 660,000 incident cases and 350,000 deaths annually, with a burden falling disproportionately on low- and middle-income regions where screening access is restricted. Although persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic human papillomavirus strains—most notably types 16 and 18, which account for roughly seventy percent of cases—serves as the primary necessary biological driver of cervical malignancy, most women clear viral infections spontaneously within two years via host immune mechanisms. This stark epidemiological difference indicates that critical secondary cofactors, specifically the local cervicovaginal microbiome microenvironment, strongly shape viral clearance, persistence, and subsequent neoplastic transformation. To rigorously examine these dynamics, researchers systematically searched PubMed from inception through September 10, 2024, focusing on cohort designs that evaluated cervicovaginal microbiota using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing or equivalent culture-independent profiling techniques at two or more serial clinical time points alongside human papillomavirus infection or cervical lesion status. Out of 1,430 identified initial records, sixty full-text articles were evaluated, culminating in twelve longitudinal investigations enrolling a cumulative total of 1,663 women across eleven countries that satisfied all methodological inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies, with resulting scores ranging from four to nine. Four studies achieved high methodological quality classifications with scores of seven or greater by establishing well-defined cohorts, clear outcome ascertainment, and controlling for critical clinical confounders; seven studies were deemed moderate quality with scores of five or six, predominantly constrained by limited confounder adjustment; and one investigation received a score of four or below due to unadjusted confounding and inadequate reporting of follow-up protocols. Because clinical and methodological parameters—including cohort demographics, follow-up durations ranging from sixteen weeks to three years, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions, and disparate community classification frameworks—exhibited substantial heterogeneity, quantitative statistical meta-analysis was not feasible. Instead, investigators conducted a structured thematic synthesis focused across three predefined scientific domains: baseline microbial community composition and corresponding clinical outcomes; community state type dynamics, transition trajectories, and temporal stability; and microbiome shifts occurring following surgical or therapeutic intervention for cervical lesions. Primary cohorts originated from diverse geographic jurisdictions, including three studies conducted in the United States, three in China, and individual studies based in the Netherlands, Sweden, South Africa, Costa Rica, the United Kingdom, and Italy. In their analytical syntheses, authors identified that baseline cervicovaginal dominance by Lactobacillus species yielded highly consistent positive evidence for both high-risk human papillomavirus clearance and the clinical regression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia across cohorts. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding Across baseline compositional analyses, cohorts revealed that elevated relative abundance of Lactobacillus crispatus and low overall alpha-diversity correlated with a significantly lower prospective risk of squamous intraepithelial lesion progression among high-risk papillomavirus-positive individuals. In cohorts from the United States, Costa Rica, and South Africa, women presenting with grade 2 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia whose baseline cervicovaginal microenvironment was Lactobacillus-dominated demonstrated significantly higher likelihoods of achieving spontaneous lesion regression at twelve and twenty-four months compared to individuals colonized by depleted communities. Conversely, women exhibiting persistent or incident cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse displayed heightened markers of anaerobic dysbiosis at both baseline and study endpoints relative to persistently negative or transiently infected participants. Specifically, baseline colonization with anaerobic taxa including Gardnerella vaginalis and Prevotella amnii predicted disease progression in Costa Rica, while independent prospective cohorts from China linked genera like Atopobium, Sneathia, and Enterococcus with viral persistence, and Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, and Klebsiella with progressive dysplasia. The evaluation of longitudinal transition patterns demonstrated that Lactobacillus-dominated community state types consistently exhibited superior temporal stability across serial samplings, whereas Lactobacillus-depleted communities underwent markedly elevated transition frequencies. In longitudinal follow-ups of human papillomavirus type 16 infections, individuals experiencing persistent viral carriage and high-grade lesion progression displayed significantly more inter-cluster transitions over eighteen months compared to participants who cleared infection. Critically, divergent transition directionality differentiated clinical trajectories: patients achieving cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 regression predominantly shifted from depleted state IV profiles into Lactobacillus iners-dominated state III communities over time, whereas non-regressing individuals consistently shifted in the opposing direction, moving away from lactobacilli toward highly diverse anaerobic states. Investigations utilizing biweekly self-sampling over sixteen weeks confirmed that communities dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus and Lactobacillus gasseri experienced the fewest transitions, underscoring crispatus dominance as the most durable and stable ecological profile. The review also examined microbial alterations occurring among participants undergoing interventions such as loop electrosurgical excision procedures, cervical excision, interferon therapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy across five treatment-focused investigations. Among women undergoing loop excision, fifty-six percent maintained their community state type between baseline treatment and their six-month clinical visit; among individuals whose profiles shifted, fifty-six percent transited between alternative Lactobacillus-dominant states, twenty-four percent transitioned from depleted states into protective Lactobacillus dominance, and twenty percent progressed toward dysbiosis. In an Italian cohort, Lactobacillus crispatus abundance rose notably following surgical excision in both high-grade lesion groups, escalating from thirty-nine to forty-five percent in grade 2 lesions and more sharply from sixteen to twenty-nine percent in grade 3 lesions. In Chinese cohorts, surgical and interferon interventions frequently spurred transitions from depleted states into Lactobacillus iners profiles, and individuals maintaining community stability following chemoradiotherapy exhibited no cancer recurrence, indicating that intervention typically facilitates an immediate partial ecological restoration. A critical focus of the synthesis centered on the complex and disputed ecological role of Lactobacillus iners, which exhibited divergent clinical correlations across the literature. While cross-sectional epidemiological studies frequently link iners dominance to higher risk of papillomavirus carriage relative to crispatus dominance, longitudinal data synthesized in this review documented that prior Lactobacillus iners dominance frequently preceded papillomavirus clearance and correlated with high community stability after excisional lesion therapy. Ecologically, Lactobacillus iners appears to occupy an intermediate transitional niche: it tolerates variable pH levels and anaerobic fluctuations far better than Lactobacillus crispatus, permitting rapid mucosal recolonization following dysbiotic disruption and serving as a functional stepping-stone toward crispatus restoration. Nevertheless, in immunocompromised cohorts, such as women living with human immunodeficiency virus, iners communities displayed pronounced ecological instability, and laboratory data indicate that iners strains can suppress mucosal defense peptides, emphasizing that its prognostic impact is highly context-dependent and governed by host immune competence and surrounding microbial taxa. Biologically, protective Lactobacillus taxa sustain an acidic cervicovaginal environment below pH 4.5 through lactic acid generation, which suppresses oncogenic human papillomavirus E6 and E7 oncoprotein transcription in laboratory experiments, while bacteriocins and hydrogen peroxide production suppress pathogenic anaerobic colonization. In contrast, dysbiotic bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis synthesize destructive proteases and sialidases that degrade mucosal protective barriers and lower secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor concentrations, fostering an inflammatory cytokine environment marked by elevated interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha that impairs localized immune responses. Furthermore, the relationship between papillomavirus and the cervicovaginal ecosystem appears fundamentally bidirectional: the viral E7 oncoprotein impairs mucosal NF-kappaB and Wnt/beta-catenin pathways, attenuating host antimicrobial peptides essential for lactobacilli persistence. This bidirectional mechanism creates an adverse biological feedback loop wherein microbial dysbiosis promotes viral persistence, which progressively reinforces mucosal dysbiosis and facilitates oncogenic dysplasia. Despite these informative findings, the systematic review highlighted severe methodological limitations across the published literature that constrain conclusive causal determinations. The authors emphasized that their search was restricted solely to PubMed and carried out by a single reviewer, introducing potential study selection biases. Methodological heterogeneity was widespread: included cohorts classified vaginal microbiota using between three and seven community state types, frequently aggregating disparate anaerobic microbiomes into a single generic classification and masking species-level nuances. Additionally, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions such as V1-V3, V3-V4, and V4 compromised direct comparisons, while infrequent sampling intervals ranging up to annual visits risked missing rapid intermediate community fluctuations. Most importantly, only two of the twelve investigations formally adjusted for critical confounding variables, including sexual activity, antibiotic administration, ethnicity, hormonal contraception, or concurrent human immunodeficiency virus status, leaving residual behavioral confounding as an alternative explanation for many reported associations. Ultimately, the review emphasizes that current observational evidence does not support the implementation of microbiome-directed interventions, such as commercial probiotics, prebiotics, or vaginal microbiome transplantation, within routine clinical papillomavirus monitoring or dysplasia management. While mechanistic studies demonstrate theoretical biological plausibility for targeted bacterial therapies, robust randomized controlled clinical trials evaluating validated cervical neoplastic outcomes remain entirely absent. The authors conclude that future research must establish harmonized classification frameworks, utilize standardized sampling intervals of three months or shorter, and employ comprehensive shotgun metagenomic sequencing capable of strain-level resolution and functional metabolic pathway analysis. Longitudinal investigations that rigorously control for behavioral determinants and host immunology will be essential to establish whether maintaining a stable, protective cervicovaginal microenvironment can be translated into targeted, evidence-based preventive therapies against cervical malignancy. Laryngeal cancer predominantly affects elderly male individuals with prolonged histories of tobacco and alcohol consumption, making its occurrence in young female individuals exceptionally uncommon. In this newly reported brief report, researchers evaluated a young Han Chinese patient presenting with persistent hoarseness who possessed no history of smoking, alcohol use, or radiation exposure. Comprehensive diagnostic testing revealed the presence of high-risk viral DNA within tumor tissue alongside objective ambulatory evidence of acidic reflux reaching the upper airway, highlighting potential non-traditional pathogenic contributors in atypical head and neck squamous neoplasms. Laryngeal malignancy represents one of the most frequent tumors of the head and neck, displaying sharp epidemiological variations across demographic categories. Disease incidence typically increases markedly after age fifty and reaches peak levels beyond sixty-five years of age, reflecting decades of cumulative exposure to inhaled tobacco smoke and ethanol. Reported male-to-female incidence ratios range between 6.4 to 1 and 24.2 to 1 in established epidemiological literature. Furthermore, anatomical distribution patterns differ between sexes, with supraglottic lesions occurring more frequently in women, followed subsequently by glottic lesions. Given that estrogen declines after menopause have been suggested to alter female biological susceptibility, early-onset glottic carcinoma in young women devoid of classic lifestyle exposures remains an extraordinarily unusual clinical presentation. The patient presented with a primary complaint of persistent hoarseness of insidious onset that had progressively worsened over more than four months beginning in January 2025. She was admitted on April 22, 2025, with an unremarkable medical background that lacked chronic hypertension, diabetes, or earlier viral infections. Physical and historical evaluations confirmed an absence of prior cytotoxic therapy, radiation exposure, or family history of head and neck cancers. Prior to her evaluation at the reporting medical center, an outside laryngoscopic examination in March 2025 identified a left vocal fold mass, leading to an initial supported laryngoscopic resection on April 1. Pathological review of that surgical specimen demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma in situ, prompting referral for specialized intervention to establish clear surgical margins. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding Specialized re-evaluation at the tertiary outpatient clinic confirmed mild congestion across both vocal folds, incomplete glottic closure, and a visible leukomembranous attachment situated at the anterior to middle portion of the left vocal cord while maintaining vocal cord mobility. Review of histological preparations revealed squamous epithelial carcinoma in situ defined by severe dysplasia, papillary growth, mitotic figures, and enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei. Subsequent immunohistochemical profiling showed mottled p16 expression, intact wild-type p53 protein levels, epidermal growth factor receptor scoring of 2+, and a Ki-67 proliferative index reaching approximately thirty percent. Preoperative laryngeal magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated slight focal swelling of the left vocal fold without invasive extension into surrounding soft tissue or cervical lymphadenopathy. To investigate underlying oncogenic alterations, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue samples underwent dedicated virological testing using the Lcn polymerase chain reaction method. The molecular assay yielded positive detection for high-risk HPV18 DNA within the tumor specimen. To determine whether secondary somatic mutations contributed to malignant transformation in the absence of external carcinogens, investigators executed targeted next-generation sequencing across a panel of 535 cancer-related genes. The comprehensive genomic panel detected no actionable somatic driver mutations, no elevation in tumor mutation burden, and no microsatellite instability, indicating that standard genomic driver mechanisms common to smoking-related head and neck cancers were entirely absent in this young non-smoking patient. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Higher HPV16 Viral Load Correlates With Severity of Cervical Squamous Lesions by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Higher HPV16 Viral Load Correlates With Severity of Cervical Squamous Lesions Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective investigation of 3,838 women who underwent high-risk human papillomavirus testing and subsequent histopathological examination has established that higher viral loads of human papillomavirus type 16 correlate significantly with increasing severity of cervical squamous lesions. Conducted by researchers using clinical records from Qilu Hospital of Shandong University between January 2018 and August 2022, the investigation evaluated the cycle threshold values generated by the automated Cobas 4800 platform as indirect, inverse measures of initial viral DNA concentration. The data demonstrated that cycle threshold values for human papillomavirus type 16 decreased progressively as diagnoses shifted from normal cervical epithelium to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. This negative correlation between cycle threshold numbers and histological severity remained robust in patients harboring solitary human papillomavirus type 16 infections as well as in patients presenting with multiple concurrent high-risk infections. In contrast, viral load measurements for human papillomavirus type 18 and twelve other pooled high-risk genotypes demonstrated no consistent quantitative correlation across histological lesion categories, underscoring pronounced genotype-dependent biological distinctions in cervical squamous pathogenesis. The study cohort was drawn from an initial pool of 86,044 patients who received Cobas 4800 high-risk human papillomavirus screening during the multi-year study interval. To isolate the relationship between baseline viral measurements and immediate histological status, the investigators applied stringent exclusion criteria that eliminated individuals with a prior history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cervical cancer, those who had previously undergone cervical physical therapy, surgical cervical procedures, or pelvic radiotherapy, and women who had received a hysterectomy. Eligibility was restricted to patients who received definitive histopathological evaluation within three months of their molecular viral test. This selection process yielded 3,838 eligible female participants with a mean age of 41.64 years, spanning an age range from 16 to 83 years. Among these evaluated participants, histopathology identified 1,660 individuals with normal cervical epithelium, 900 women with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1, 1,019 patients with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or grade 3, and 259 individuals diagnosed with invasive squamous cell carcinoma. The protocol was formally approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Qilu Hospital, Shandong University. To safeguard diagnostic accuracy and biological sample integrity, all participating patients were required to follow specific pre-sampling clinical preparation guidelines prior to presenting for examination. These instructions prohibited vaginal douching, the administration of topical vaginal medications such as suppositories, and physical cervical therapy for at least 72 hours before cervical sampling occurred. In addition, participants were instructed to abstain from sexual intercourse for a minimum of 24 hours prior to sample collection, and all collection appointments were strictly scheduled outside active menstrual bleeding intervals. Trained gynecologists obtained the cervical cellular specimens using specialized sampling devices under aseptic conditions. Specimen handling, chemical preservation, and subsequent automated molecular runs were executed in strict accordance with manufacturer protocols provided by Roche Diagnostics. Every test run was conducted within the same institutional laboratory environment to eliminate inter-facility diagnostic drift, and all analytical outputs were supervised and interpreted by certified molecular diagnostics technicians. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding The molecular assessment relied on the Cobas 4800 system, an assay approved by the Food and Drug Administration that combines real-time fluorescence-based quantitative polymerase chain reaction with selective nucleic acid hybridization. The platform isolates cellular and viral DNA through automated extraction before executing multiplex PCR amplification using primers specific to high-risk human papillomavirus regions and human cellular beta-globin. A four-channel optical detection array captures fluorescence signals, employing FAM dye for human papillomavirus type 16, HEX dye for type 18, CY5 dye for the twelve other pooled high-risk types, and ROX dye for beta-globin, which serves as an internal quality control to confirm specimen cellular adequacy and screen for polymerase chain reaction inhibitors. The instrument monitors amplification kinetics to register the cycle threshold, representing the exact amplification cycle at which fluorescent emissions exceed background thresholds. Because cycle threshold numbers maintain an inverse linear relationship with logarithmic starting copy concentrations of viral target DNA, lower cycle numbers directly denote higher initial viral loads. Clinical cutoffs established by the manufacturer designated reactions as positive when cycle threshold readings fell at or below 40.5 for type 16, 40.0 for type 18, and 40.0 for the pooled genotype channel. Histopathological diagnoses were established within a mean turnaround interval of 13.03 days following the initial molecular test, with 89.42 percent of the cohort completing full histological evaluations within one month of molecular screening. Pathological classifications were derived from consensus reviews conducted independently by two senior gynecologic pathologists who examined tissue samples obtained through colposcopy-directed punch biopsies, loop electrosurgical excision procedures, cold knife conization, or therapeutic hysterectomy procedures. When individual participants had multiple surgical specimens or repeated histological diagnoses, the most severe diagnostic classification was selected for statistical analysis. Pathological grading followed the World Health Organization Classification of Tumors of the Female Reproductive System, establishing four primary analytical strata: normal histology, low-grade dysplasia designated as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1, high-grade intraepithelial lesions combining grades 2 and 3, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Statistical testing conducted via SPSS software version 26.0 utilized two-sided tests, establishing significance at P values below 0.05, and relied exclusively on non-parametric approaches, including Kruskal-Wallis tests with Bonferroni post hoc adjustments and Spearman rank correlations, due to the exponential relationship governing cycle threshold measurements. Overall high-risk human papillomavirus positivity across the 3,838 participants reached 78.3 percent, with positive detection rates scaling from 61.4 percent in the histologically normal group to 87.2 percent in cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1, 94.0 percent in grades 2 and 3, and 93.1 percent in invasive squamous cell carcinoma, with all diseased categories significantly exceeding normal baseline positivity rates at P values below 0.001. The prevalence of human papillomavirus type 16 exhibited a pronounced upward trend across progressive histological stages, rising from 16.8 percent in normal specimens to 23.8 percent in grade 1 lesions, 53.2 percent in grades 2 and 3, and 75.7 percent in squamous cell carcinomas. Conversely, detection of the twelve pooled non-16 and non-18 high-risk types peaked at 56.1 percent within cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1, but dropped to 38.3 percent in normal tissues, 36.1 percent in advanced intraepithelial lesions, and only 14.3 percent in invasive squamous cancers. Type 18 positivity remained consistently low across all histological categories, with the combined grade 2 and 3 category demonstrating a significantly lower positive rate than the normal and grade 1 groups, while revealing no significant frequency differences across the remaining diagnostic comparisons. Quantitative viral load analyses revealed that among the 858 women diagnosed with solitary human papillomavirus type 16 infections, cycle threshold values showed a statistically significant negative correlation with histological severity across the spectrum from normal tissues to invasive malignancy, yielding a Spearman correlation coefficient of negative 0.386 at a P value below 0.001. Pairwise statistical comparisons confirmed significant viral load increments as histological abnormalities worsened, although no significant difference in cycle threshold numbers emerged between the high-grade intraepithelial cohort and the invasive squamous cell carcinoma group, where the comparative P value reached 0.157. Among the 152 patients presenting with isolated type 18 infections, cycle threshold measurements exhibited no significant variation across lesion grades, yielding a P value of 0.746. In the 1,545 individuals testing positive for the twelve other pooled high-risk types, the correlation between cycle threshold numbers and histological severity proved remarkably weak, characterized by a correlation coefficient of negative 0.134. Although cycle threshold values for the pooled types were significantly lower in grade 1 and grade 2 or 3 lesions relative to normal tissues, no significant differences appeared across any other histological category comparisons. When examining multiple concurrent viral infections, the researchers observed that human papillomavirus type 16 maintained its negative cycle threshold trajectory, demonstrating an inverse correlation coefficient of negative 0.416 with lesion severity at a P value below 0.001. In contrast, co-infections involving type 18 continued to exhibit no significant variation in cycle threshold values across histological stages, producing a non-significant P value of 0.235. Notably, when the authors compared cycle threshold values for both type 16 and type 18 between single-infection patients and multiple-infection patients within identical histological lesion categories, no statistically significant differences emerged across any pathological stage, indicating that inter-genotypic co-existence does not measurably alter viral replication levels. To evaluate the clinical utility of cycle threshold measurements for discriminating high-grade pathology, receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was conducted on solitary type 16 cases. This analysis identified an optimal cycle threshold cutoff value of 32.25 for detecting lesions graded as intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse, producing an area under the curve of 0.72 with an 80.7 percent sensitivity and a 54.4 percent specificity. Binary logistic regression and single-factor analyses demonstrated that multiple viral infections did not heighten the risk of severe dysplasia beyond that observed in solitary type 16 infection. Solitary human papillomavirus type 16 infection exhibited the highest proportion of high-grade lesions at 62.7 percent. When type 16 was accompanied by type 18, high-grade lesion frequency was comparable at 62.5 percent, whereas co-infections combining type 16 with the pooled high-risk types, or type 16 with both type 18 and pooled types, demonstrated significantly decreased adjusted odds ratios of 0.731 and 0.281, respectively. Solitary type 18 infection presented a baseline high-grade lesion proportion of 20.4 percent, which increased only when co-occurring with type 16 or pooled types. Analysis of patient age demonstrated that chronological age was not an independent risk factor for high-grade dysplasia in logistic models, yielding an odds ratio of 1.001. However, within the cohort of patients positive for type 16 who presented with grade 2 or 3 lesions, individuals aged 50 years or older exhibited significantly lower cycle threshold values, indicating higher viral loads, than patients younger than 30 years and those between 30 and 39 years. The study authors highlighted several biological and methodological explanations for these observed patterns, while explicitly acknowledging important study limitations. The tight link between viral load and histological severity in human papillomavirus type 16 likely reflects sustained episomal viral replication during squamous lesion progression, whereas type 18 is biologically prone to early genomic integration and is predominantly associated with glandular adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma. Methodologically, the pooled detection of twelve non-16 and non-18 high-risk types in the Cobas 4800 system prevents individual genotype quantification and may obscure type-specific load variations. Furthermore, cycle threshold outputs remain semi-quantitative surrogates that can be influenced by sampling cellularity, swab pressure, and variable amplification efficiencies. Because the study utilized a retrospective cross-sectional framework without longitudinal tracking, the reported findings reflect statistical associations rather than proven causal mechanisms of disease progression. Finally, the authors noted that unmeasured confounding factors, including host immune status, sexual behavior, and human papillomavirus vaccination coverage, were unavailable, cautioning that viral load associations may differ in cohorts with high vaccination uptake. High-grade cervical lesions, designated as CIN2+, are critical precursors to cervical cancer. The clinical investigation specifically examined human papillomavirus infection, cervical cytology abnormalities, and vaccination status to determine their association with histopathologically confirmed disease. Conducted in an Iranian colposcopy population, the study reviewed medical records spanning a ten-year period, from January 2014 to January 2024. All 246 female participants had undergone colposcopic evaluation during this timeframe. The authors collected data on patient demographics, including age and marital status, alongside clinical characteristics, cervical cytology, human papillomavirus status, and documented HPV vaccination history. Biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ was defined as histopathologically diagnosed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, grade 3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or invasive cervical cancer. Viral testing utilized the PaxView® Kit to detect human papillomavirus and identify high-risk genotypes. To evaluate factors linked to CIN2+, investigators performed univariable and multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression analyses, reporting adjusted odds ratios and 95 percent confidence intervals. Of the 246 women analyzed in the retrospective study, 50 patients, or 20.3 percent, were diagnosed with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ lesions, while 196 women were categorized as CIN2−. Among the 50 women with CIN2+, 37 cases, or 74.0 percent, were classified as CIN2, and 10 cases, or 20.0 percent, were CIN3. Adenocarcinoma in situ was identified in 2 women, representing 4.0 percent, and invasive cervical cancer was diagnosed in 1 patient, representing 2.0 percent. The distribution of HPV status and cytological results differed significantly between women with CIN2+ and those without, with both differences yielding p-values of less than 0.001. HPV16/18 infection appeared in 56.0 percent of women with CIN2+ compared to 28.6 percent of those in the CIN2− group. In contrast, HPV-negative results were observed in 18.0 percent of the CIN2+ cohort versus 39.8 percent of CIN2− participants. Cytology showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, or HSIL, was recorded in 38.0 percent of CIN2+ cases compared with 10.7 percent of CIN2− cases. In addition, an absence of HPV vaccination was documented in 42.0 percent of the CIN2+ group versus 16.8 percent of women in the comparison group. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression demonstrated that three key factors were independently associated with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+. HPV16/18 infection yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 3.94, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.70 to 9.74 and a p-value of 0.001. Lack of HPV vaccination was associated with higher odds of CIN2+, showing an adjusted odds ratio of 2.20, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.03 to 4.65 and a p-value of 0.042. Women with HSIL cytology exhibited higher odds of CIN2+ than those with normal cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, designated as NILM, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.84, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.09 to 7.54 and a p-value of 0.031. Age, marital status, and other high-risk HPV genotypes showed no statistically significant independent association with CIN2+. The investigators noted that the observed association between the lack of HPV vaccination and higher odds of CIN2+ requires cautious interpretation by clinicians and researchers. Because vaccination timing relative to initial HPV exposure was not recorded in the retrospective dataset, the finding could reflect unmeasured confounding parameters. Prospective studies examining vaccination timing and pre-vaccination HPV status are required to clarify this relationship. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive systematic review synthesizing twelve longitudinal studies across eleven countries has revealed that the temporal stability of Lactobacillus-dominated microbial communities in the cervicovaginal tract is the most consistent microbiome feature associated with human papillomavirus clearance and the regression of cervical pre-cancerous lesions. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the investigation systematically examined how dynamic shifts across community state types correlate with viral persistence, viral clearance, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia transitions over time. Cervical cancer represents the fourth most common malignancy in women worldwide, responsible for an estimated 660,000 incident cases and 350,000 deaths annually, with a burden falling disproportionately on low- and middle-income regions where screening access is restricted. Although persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic human papillomavirus strains—most notably types 16 and 18, which account for roughly seventy percent of cases—serves as the primary necessary biological driver of cervical malignancy, most women clear viral infections spontaneously within two years via host immune mechanisms. This stark epidemiological difference indicates that critical secondary cofactors, specifically the local cervicovaginal microbiome microenvironment, strongly shape viral clearance, persistence, and subsequent neoplastic transformation. To rigorously examine these dynamics, researchers systematically searched PubMed from inception through September 10, 2024, focusing on cohort designs that evaluated cervicovaginal microbiota using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing or equivalent culture-independent profiling techniques at two or more serial clinical time points alongside human papillomavirus infection or cervical lesion status. Out of 1,430 identified initial records, sixty full-text articles were evaluated, culminating in twelve longitudinal investigations enrolling a cumulative total of 1,663 women across eleven countries that satisfied all methodological inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies, with resulting scores ranging from four to nine. Four studies achieved high methodological quality classifications with scores of seven or greater by establishing well-defined cohorts, clear outcome ascertainment, and controlling for critical clinical confounders; seven studies were deemed moderate quality with scores of five or six, predominantly constrained by limited confounder adjustment; and one investigation received a score of four or below due to unadjusted confounding and inadequate reporting of follow-up protocols. Because clinical and methodological parameters—including cohort demographics, follow-up durations ranging from sixteen weeks to three years, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions, and disparate community classification frameworks—exhibited substantial heterogeneity, quantitative statistical meta-analysis was not feasible. Instead, investigators conducted a structured thematic synthesis focused across three predefined scientific domains: baseline microbial community composition and corresponding clinical outcomes; community state type dynamics, transition trajectories, and temporal stability; and microbiome shifts occurring following surgical or therapeutic intervention for cervical lesions. Primary cohorts originated from diverse geographic jurisdictions, including three studies conducted in the United States, three in China, and individual studies based in the Netherlands, Sweden, South Africa, Costa Rica, the United Kingdom, and Italy. In their analytical syntheses, authors identified that baseline cervicovaginal dominance by Lactobacillus species yielded highly consistent positive evidence for both high-risk human papillomavirus clearance and the clinical regression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia across cohorts. Across baseline compositional analyses, cohorts revealed that elevated relative abundance of Lactobacillus crispatus and low overall alpha-diversity correlated with a significantly lower prospective risk of squamous intraepithelial lesion progression among high-risk papillomavirus-positive individuals. In cohorts from the United States, Costa Rica, and South Africa, women presenting with grade 2 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia whose baseline cervicovaginal microenvironment was Lactobacillus-dominated demonstrated significantly higher likelihoods of achieving spontaneous lesion regression at twelve and twenty-four months compared to individuals colonized by depleted communities. Conversely, women exhibiting persistent or incident cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse displayed heightened markers of anaerobic dysbiosis at both baseline and study endpoints relative to persistently negative or transiently infected participants. Specifically, baseline colonization with anaerobic taxa including Gardnerella vaginalis and Prevotella amnii predicted disease progression in Costa Rica, while independent prospective cohorts from China linked genera like Atopobium, Sneathia, and Enterococcus with viral persistence, and Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, and Klebsiella with progressive dysplasia. The evaluation of longitudinal transition patterns demonstrated that Lactobacillus-dominated community state types consistently exhibited superior temporal stability across serial samplings, whereas Lactobacillus-depleted communities underwent markedly elevated transition frequencies. In longitudinal follow-ups of human papillomavirus type 16 infections, individuals experiencing persistent viral carriage and high-grade lesion progression displayed significantly more inter-cluster transitions over eighteen months compared to participants who cleared infection. Critically, divergent transition directionality differentiated clinical trajectories: patients achieving cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 regression predominantly shifted from depleted state IV profiles into Lactobacillus iners-dominated state III communities over time, whereas non-regressing individuals consistently shifted in the opposing direction, moving away from lactobacilli toward highly diverse anaerobic states. Investigations utilizing biweekly self-sampling over sixteen weeks confirmed that communities dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus and Lactobacillus gasseri experienced the fewest transitions, underscoring crispatus dominance as the most durable and stable ecological profile. The review also examined microbial alterations occurring among participants undergoing interventions such as loop electrosurgical excision procedures, cervical excision, interferon therapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy across five treatment-focused investigations. Among women undergoing loop excision, fifty-six percent maintained their community state type between baseline treatment and their six-month clinical visit; among individuals whose profiles shifted, fifty-six percent transited between alternative Lactobacillus-dominant states, twenty-four percent transitioned from depleted states into protective Lactobacillus dominance, and twenty percent progressed toward dysbiosis. In an Italian cohort, Lactobacillus crispatus abundance rose notably following surgical excision in both high-grade lesion groups, escalating from thirty-nine to forty-five percent in grade 2 lesions and more sharply from sixteen to twenty-nine percent in grade 3 lesions. In Chinese cohorts, surgical and interferon interventions frequently spurred transitions from depleted states into Lactobacillus iners profiles, and individuals maintaining community stability following chemoradiotherapy exhibited no cancer recurrence, indicating that intervention typically facilitates an immediate partial ecological restoration. A critical focus of the synthesis centered on the complex and disputed ecological role of Lactobacillus iners, which exhibited divergent clinical correlations across the literature. While cross-sectional epidemiological studies frequently link iners dominance to higher risk of papillomavirus carriage relative to crispatus dominance, longitudinal data synthesized in this review documented that prior Lactobacillus iners dominance frequently preceded papillomavirus clearance and correlated with high community stability after excisional lesion therapy. Ecologically, Lactobacillus iners appears to occupy an intermediate transitional niche: it tolerates variable pH levels and anaerobic fluctuations far better than Lactobacillus crispatus, permitting rapid mucosal recolonization following dysbiotic disruption and serving as a functional stepping-stone toward crispatus restoration. Nevertheless, in immunocompromised cohorts, such as women living with human immunodeficiency virus, iners communities displayed pronounced ecological instability, and laboratory data indicate that iners strains can suppress mucosal defense peptides, emphasizing that its prognostic impact is highly context-dependent and governed by host immune competence and surrounding microbial taxa. Biologically, protective Lactobacillus taxa sustain an acidic cervicovaginal environment below pH 4.5 through lactic acid generation, which suppresses oncogenic human papillomavirus E6 and E7 oncoprotein transcription in laboratory experiments, while bacteriocins and hydrogen peroxide production suppress pathogenic anaerobic colonization. In contrast, dysbiotic bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis synthesize destructive proteases and sialidases that degrade mucosal protective barriers and lower secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor concentrations, fostering an inflammatory cytokine environment marked by elevated interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha that impairs localized immune responses. Furthermore, the relationship between papillomavirus and the cervicovaginal ecosystem appears fundamentally bidirectional: the viral E7 oncoprotein impairs mucosal NF-kappaB and Wnt/beta-catenin pathways, attenuating host antimicrobial peptides essential for lactobacilli persistence. This bidirectional mechanism creates an adverse biological feedback loop wherein microbial dysbiosis promotes viral persistence, which progressively reinforces mucosal dysbiosis and facilitates oncogenic dysplasia. Despite these informative findings, the systematic review highlighted severe methodological limitations across the published literature that constrain conclusive causal determinations. The authors emphasized that their search was restricted solely to PubMed and carried out by a single reviewer, introducing potential study selection biases. Methodological heterogeneity was widespread: included cohorts classified vaginal microbiota using between three and seven community state types, frequently aggregating disparate anaerobic microbiomes into a single generic classification and masking species-level nuances. Additionally, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions such as V1-V3, V3-V4, and V4 compromised direct comparisons, while infrequent sampling intervals ranging up to annual visits risked missing rapid intermediate community fluctuations. Most importantly, only two of the twelve investigations formally adjusted for critical confounding variables, including sexual activity, antibiotic administration, ethnicity, hormonal contraception, or concurrent human immunodeficiency virus status, leaving residual behavioral confounding as an alternative explanation for many reported associations. Ultimately, the review emphasizes that current observational evidence does not support the implementation of microbiome-directed interventions, such as commercial probiotics, prebiotics, or vaginal microbiome transplantation, within routine clinical papillomavirus monitoring or dysplasia management. While mechanistic studies demonstrate theoretical biological plausibility for targeted bacterial therapies, robust randomized controlled clinical trials evaluating validated cervical neoplastic outcomes remain entirely absent. The authors conclude that future research must establish harmonized classification frameworks, utilize standardized sampling intervals of three months or shorter, and employ comprehensive shotgun metagenomic sequencing capable of strain-level resolution and functional metabolic pathway analysis. Longitudinal investigations that rigorously control for behavioral determinants and host immunology will be essential to establish whether maintaining a stable, protective cervicovaginal microenvironment can be translated into targeted, evidence-based preventive therapies against cervical malignancy. supplementary_news.content_title: CATIE - Canada's source for HIV and hepatitis C information
supplementary_news.content: Background information on HIV, hepatitis C and STIs in Canada, including basic information, statistics (epidemiology), provincial and national strategies to address HIV, hepatitis C and STIs, and social determinants of health. Information on HIV and hepatitis C transmission and prevention, including STIs and safer sex, harm reduction, pregnancy and infant feeding, and microbicides and vaccines. Information on diagnostic tests for HIV, hepatitis C and STIs; the delivery of testing and counselling; and resources for people who are newly diagnosed. Information on treatment, care and support for HIV, hepatitis C and STIs, including medications, healthy living, pregnancy and infant feeding, hepatitis C re-infection, and long-term health issues. CATIE is Canada’s source for HIV and hepatitis C information, and so much more. We increase knowledge about sexual health and substance use, we build the capacity of service providers to deliver prevention, testing and treatment services, and we promote policies and programs proven to work based on research, practice and lived experience. Very high rates of hepatitis C virus (HCV) cure observed among immigrants to Canada Canadians with hepatitis C have historically had worse outcomes if born outside the country. Researchers reviewed data from 17 clinics to compare patients born in and outside Canada. When provided treatment, immigrant patients had comparable or superior health outcomes. Canadian study finds low rates of vaccination against human papillomavirus among women living with HIV Women with HIV are at increased risk for cervical cancer, caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). An analysis of 505 Canadian women with HIV found that only 47% had received HPV vaccination. Researchers called for greater efforts to increase HPV vaccination rates in this population. CATIE strengthens Canada’s response to HIV, hepatitis C and the toxic drug crisis by bridging research and practice. We connect healthcare and community-based service providers with the latest science, and promote good practices for prevention, testing, treatment and substance use health programs

The majority of hrHPV infections are transient events that resolve without causing neoplastic change, whereas only a small minority persist over time, acquire transforming activity, and progress toward cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) or grade 3 or worse (CIN3+). Because high-risk viral detection alone cannot distinguish between self-limiting infections and progressive lesions, clinicians require robust triage strategies. Such triage mechanisms are vital to identify the specific subset of women who genuinely require immediate colposcopy or intensified clinical surveillance, while simultaneously protecting others from unnecessary referrals, psychological burden, and procedural overtreatment. To clarify how emerging molecular tools might meet these clinical demands, a structured narrative review published in Infectious Agents and Cancer evaluates the clinical readiness of biomarker-integrated triage following positive hrHPV screening. The analysis evaluates candidate diagnostic markers across three biologically distinct dimensions: viral oncogenic activity, host-cell transformation, and the local immune microenvironment. Rather than evaluating markers in isolation, the authors explore whether integrating these biological layers can refine patient risk assessment after a positive screening result. Throughout the evaluation, the review maintains that candidate biomarkers cannot be validated on the strength of biological associations alone; instead, their clinical value depends entirely on whether they measurably improve risk-based clinical management in real-world cervical screening. Focusing on viral oncogenic activity, the review investigates testing for HPV E6/E7 messenger RNA (mRNA), which directly reflects active viral oncogene transcription within host cervical tissue. In selected assay-specific and population-specific settings, evaluating viral E6/E7 mRNA transcription can achieve higher clinical specificity than standard HPV DNA testing by differentiating active transforming infection from inconsequential viral carriage. Nonetheless, the authors highlight significant diagnostic caveats that currently limit uncritical adoption. Commercial mRNA assays are not interchangeable in their diagnostic performance characteristics. Most importantly, a negative mRNA result cannot independently exclude the presence of CIN2+ or CIN3+ lesions, demonstrating that negative test results are insufficient to rule out high-grade cervical precancer on their own. These analytical complexities are further compounded when mRNA testing is applied outside conventional clinician-collected sampling protocols. In self-collected mRNA workflows, evaluations reveal that certain combinations of collection devices and analytical assays exhibit reduced clinical sensitivity compared to standard clinician-obtained cervical samples. Because diagnostic accuracy may degrade under specific self-sampling conditions, the review emphasizes that findings cannot be generalized across platforms. Consequently, any proposed self-collection workflow mandates separate, rigorous clinical validation tailored to the precise device, assay chemistry, and operational laboratory protocol employed before it can be safely introduced into routine triage. The second major dimension addressed in the review centers on host-cell transformation biomarkers, represented primarily by host DNA methylation panels including PAX1 and JAM3. These molecular assays capture critical transformation-associated epigenetic alterations that occur as infected host cells undergo neoplastic changes. According to the review, host DNA methylation testing offers substantial promise for refining cancer risk among specific patient populations that present diagnostic dilemmas under existing protocols. These target populations include women infected with non-16/18 hrHPV genotypes, individuals experiencing persistent hrHPV positivity despite negative cytology results, and patients presenting with borderline cytological abnormalities. However, widespread clinical applicability remains contingent upon formal assay standardization, rigorous threshold validation, multi-center external validation, and direct comparative studies against established triage methods. In the third dimension, the review examines immune-context markers, with particular focus on interleukin-17-related indicators that provide mechanistic insight into inflammatory activation, impaired viral clearance, and cervical tissue remodeling. Although these immunological indicators offer valuable conceptual understanding regarding host-virus interactions and immune dysregulation in the cervix, the available body of evidence remains predominantly exploratory. The authors caution that critical implementation metrics—including laboratory assay reproducibility, clinical workflow feasibility, overall cost-effectiveness, and demonstrable real-world clinical utility—remain insufficiently established to support the routine clinical adoption of immune markers in contemporary triage algorithms. Looking forward, the review outlines prospective evaluation of stepwise virus–host triage models against guideline-relevant comparators as a valuable near-term research direction. The authors note that emerging multi-biomarker strategies must be directly compared against existing clinical standards, including HPV16/18 or extended genotyping, conventional reflex cytology, and p16/Ki-67 dual-stain testing. Successful translation of any biomarker panel into clinical practice will ultimately demand platform-specific validation, standardized clinical thresholds, longitudinal evaluation of surveillance safety and missed CIN3+ lesions, formal decision-curve modeling, and detailed cost-effectiveness analyses. Only through such rigorous, evidence-based demonstration of net clinical benefit can novel biomarker-integrated approaches successfully improve patient management following positive hrHPV screening. Vaccine effectiveness exceeded 97% across all four treatment groups. Single-dose vaccination could simplify immunisation programmes and improve global vaccine access. A SINGLE DOSE of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine provides protection against high-risk HPV infections comparable to a two-dose regimen, according to findings from a large randomised trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The results could have important implications for global vaccination strategies, potentially simplifying immunisation programmes and improving access to cervical cancer prevention. The ESCUDDO trial investigated whether one dose of HPV vaccination was noninferior to two doses in preventing persistent infections with HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancers worldwide. Although multidose HPV vaccination is highly effective, global uptake remains uneven, with barriers including vaccine availability, cost, and difficulties completing vaccination schedules. Researchers sought to determine whether a single-dose approach could provide comparable protection while reducing the resources required for vaccination programmes. Single-Dose Vaccination Achieves Over 97% Effectiveness The randomised trial enrolled 20,330 girls aged 12–16 years, who were assigned to receive either one or two doses of a bivalent HPV vaccine or one or two doses of a nonavalent HPV vaccine. The primary endpoint was a new HPV16 or HPV18 infection occurring between months 12 and 60 that persisted for at least 6 months. Researchers also assessed vaccine effectiveness by comparing infection rates among vaccinated participants with those observed in a separate, nonrandomised survey involving 3,005 unvaccinated girls and women. Results demonstrated that a single dose of either vaccine was noninferior to two doses in preventing persistent HPV16 or HPV18 infection. For the bivalent vaccine, the difference in infection rates between one and two doses was −0.13 infections per 100 participants (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.45 to 0.15; P<escape><</escape>0.001 for noninferiority). Similarly, the nonavalent vaccine demonstrated a rate difference of 0.21 infections per 100 participants (95% CI: −0.09 to 0.51; P<escape><</escape>0.001 for noninferiority). Importantly, vaccine effectiveness was at least 97% across all four vaccination groups, highlighting the high level of protection achieved with both single-dose and two-dose regimens. No safety concerns were identified during the trial. These findings provide strong evidence that administering a single HPV vaccine dose can offer comparable protection against persistent infection with HPV16 and HPV18 over the study period. The results are particularly relevant for countries where limited resources, vaccine supply constraints, or challenges accessing healthcare services may prevent adolescents from completing multidose vaccination schedules. Reducing the number of required doses could simplify vaccination delivery, lower programme costs, and allow available vaccine supplies to reach more individuals. This may be especially valuable in low- and middle-income countries, where the burden of cervical cancer remains disproportionately high. However, the trial assessed persistent HPV infection rather than cervical cancer incidence, and longer-term monitoring will be important to establish the durability of protection beyond the five-year follow-up period. Overall, the researchers concluded that one dose of either the bivalent or nonavalent HPV vaccine was noninferior to two doses in preventing persistent HPV16 or HPV18 infection. The findings strengthen the evidence supporting simplified HPV vaccination schedules and could contribute to broader global efforts to prevent cervical cancer. Reference: Kreimer AR, et al. Noninferiority of One HPV Vaccine Dose to Two Doses. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(24):2421–2433. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2506765. The study evaluated nationwide vaccine coverage alongside demographic and psychosocial factors using a newly developed measurement instrument, identifying substantial disparities in vaccination rates across age, gender, marital status, and specific behavioral measures. Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection represents a major global public health burden, yet clear national policies concerning HPV vaccination remain absent in Iran despite the availability of effective vaccines. The authors noted that understanding current vaccine coverage and the precise factors that influence vaccine acceptance among Iranian adults is essential for designing and guiding effective public health interventions. To investigate these determinants, the research team conducted a cross-sectional study in 2025 utilizing an online survey administered to Iranian adults. The survey incorporated the newly developed Iranian HPV Vaccine Determinants Scale (I-HPV-VDS), an assessment tool constructed on the foundation of established health behavior frameworks. Psychometric evaluation of the instrument confirmed its validity and reliability through face validity testing, construct validity assessment, and Cronbach’s alpha reliability calculations. Discover more Book a Checkup Find Vaccines vaccines vaccine Vaccine To improve population representativeness across the national adult demographic, the investigators applied post-stratification weighting based on national distributions of age, gender, and educational attainment. The resulting weighted cohort comprised 1,416 individuals. The researchers then performed univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses to identify independent determinants associated with whether participants had received the HPV vaccine. The multivariable regression analysis identified several demographic characteristics that were significantly linked with vaccine receipt. Vaccine uptake was significantly higher among younger adults, who exhibited an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 2.88 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.52–5.47). Female respondents were also considerably more likely to be vaccinated than male respondents, with an aOR of 5.90 (95% CI: 3.09–11.26). Unmarried individuals showed the highest odds of vaccination relative to married individuals, demonstrating an aOR of 16.72 (95% CI: 7.64–36.57), a pattern driven particularly by individuals who were previously married or involved in non-marital relationships. Psychosocial constructs measured by the Iranian HPV Vaccine Determinants Scale also emerged as significant independent predictors of vaccination. Each one standard deviation increase in Social Support and Self-efficacy was associated with nearly four times higher odds of vaccine uptake (aOR: 4.46, 95% CI: 2.43–8.18). In addition, Risk Perception was associated with approximately twofold higher odds of vaccination (aOR: 2.12, 95% CI: 1.27–3.52). By contrast, other scale components did not demonstrate independent predictive power in the final models. Stigma-related elements and behavioral concern components showed no independent statistical association with HPV vaccination in the multivariable analysis. The investigators also highlighted that the wide confidence intervals observed across several demographic subgroups likely stemmed from very low event counts within specific strata combined with the post-stratification weighting, noting that these specific estimates warrant cautious interpretation. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Find Cancer Care Browse Reference Find Study Aids The authors concluded that the critically low HPV vaccination uptake observed in Iran, particularly among men, alongside pronounced social inequities, demonstrates an urgent need to evaluate access measures, including the potential inclusion of the HPV vaccine in the country’s national immunization program. They emphasized that strengthening public understanding of HPV susceptibility and vaccine effectiveness, fostering supportive social environments, and aligning with global cervical cancer elimination goals and regional vaccination initiatives remain critical priorities. The implementation of the Iranian HPV Vaccine Determinants Scale (I-HPV-VDS) marks a structured methodological approach to capturing behavioral determinants grounded in established health behavior frameworks. By integrating face validity, construct validity, and internal consistency testing using Cronbach’s alpha, the research team ensured that the survey instrument rigorously measured distinct psychosocial domains. Furthermore, the use of post-stratification weighting based on national demographic benchmarks for age, gender, and educational attainment allowed the 2025 online survey to better reflect population-level distributions, providing a standardized basis for the multivariable logistic regression models evaluating uptake. From a broader public health perspective, the findings provide empirical evidence to inform future policy decisions and national health strategies. Given that human papillomavirus vaccination plays a central role in worldwide cervical cancer elimination efforts and neighboring nations have advanced their own vaccination initiatives, establishing clear national policies in Iran represents a critical next step. The authors emphasized that addressing the low uptake, particularly among men, requires measures to improve access—including potential inclusion in the national immunization program—while strengthening public understanding of HPV susceptibility, reinforcing vaccine effectiveness, and enhancing supportive social environments.
