Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the cross-sectional investigation revealed that while overall acceptance of annual visual screening was remarkably high among clinic attendees, women who declined visual examinations frequently cited physical discomfort during pelvic examinations and expressed strong interest in alternative HPV-based testing methods, including self-collection. Cervical cancer represents a severe public health burden in low- and middle-income countries, where persistent infections with high-risk human papillomaviruses cause the majority of disease cases. In Zimbabwe, cervical cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and the leading cause of cancer mortality among women, resulting in an estimated 3,000 diagnoses and 2,200 deaths each year. The intersection of this oncologic burden with high HIV prevalence further elevates risk, as women living with HIV are six times more likely to experience persistent HPV infections that advance to high-grade cervical lesions at younger ages than their HIV-negative peers. To address this dual burden, national cervical cancer control efforts supported by the Zimbabwe Technical Assistance, Training and Education Center for Health, known as Zim-TTECH, historically scaled up annual single-visit screen-and-treat protocols using visual inspection with acetic acid and cervicography, abbreviated as VIAC. In 2023 alone, these initiatives screened 100,117 women living with HIV across 360 public facilities in five provinces. However, aligned with updated 2021 World Health Organization recommendations, Zimbabwe revised its national screening guidelines in 2023 to adopt molecular HPV DNA testing every three to five years as the primary screening tool, reserving VIAC for triage to guide treatment eligibility. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding To assess client readiness for this strategic transition, investigators administered a structured 31-item paper questionnaire between February and June 2023 to a convenience sample of 451 women living with HIV aged 18 to 49 years. The evaluation was conducted at three purposively selected public-sector facilities operated by the Ministry of Health and Child Care: Glenview Polyclinic, an urban outpatient facility in Harare; Guruve District Hospital, a rural referral facility in Mashonaland Central Province; and Tsholotsho District Hospital, serving rural communities in Matabeleland North Province. Questionnaires were administered in Shona or Ndebele by nurse interviewers who were distinct from the healthcare providers who offered or conducted the clinical examinations. Among the 451 participants who completed the assessment, 414 women, representing 91.8 percent of the cohort, accepted same-day VIAC screening, whereas 37 women, or 8.2 percent, declined the procedure. Participant demographics showed a median age of 40 years, with an interquartile range of 33 to 45 years. Most respondents demonstrated long-standing engagement with HIV care; 76.3 percent had known their HIV-positive status for five years or more, 74.5 percent had attended the participating clinic for at least five years, and 99.8 percent were receiving antiretroviral therapy. Furthermore, 73.4 percent of participants reached their respective health facilities by walking. Among the 414 women who accepted VIAC screening, 323 women, accounting for 78.0 percent, were presenting for re-screening, while 91 women, or 22.2 percent, were undergoing screening for the first time. The motivations driving uptake differed markedly based on prior screening history. Women presenting for repeat examinations primarily cited a desire to feel secure about their personal health, which accounted for 45.8 percent of responses, followed by compliance with annual screening recommendations at 39.6 percent, and encouragement from healthcare workers at 8.0 percent. Conversely, first-time screeners identified healthcare worker encouragement as their primary driver at 39.6 percent, followed by adherence to annual screening recommendations at 38.5 percent, and health reassurance at 17.6 percent. When questioned about their future screening preferences, the majority of women who accepted VIAC indicated a clear desire to continue with visual inspection rather than shift to molecular testing. Specifically, 70.3 percent of women attending re-screening and 89.0 percent of first-time screeners preferred continuing with VIAC. The authors observed that this preference likely reflected familiarity and existing trust in visual modalities, as most participants were introduced to the concepts of HPV testing and self-sampling for the first time during the questionnaire administration through a standardized explanatory script. Discover more Donate to Research Find Conferences health Health Cancer A distinct pattern emerged among the 37 women who declined VIAC screening. Despite 78.4 percent knowing their HIV status for at least five years and 73.0 percent having attended the same facility for five or more years, 75.7 percent of this group had never undergone cervical cancer screening, even though 43.2 percent had been offered screening more than once in the past. The dominant barrier to uptake was procedural apprehension: 54.1 percent cited fear of physical discomfort associated with the speculum-guided pelvic examination, 13.5 percent expressed worry regarding the potential screening result, and 10.8 percent cited perceived side effects of VIAC. Importantly, nearly half of the women who declined VIAC screening, representing 48.6 percent of the refusal group, indicated a preference for future HPV testing over visual inspection. Among the 18 hesitant women who favored HPV testing, preferences regarding specimen collection were distributed across multiple modalities: 21.6 percent favored provider-collected sampling, 16.2 percent preferred self-collection conducted at home, and 13.6 percent preferred self-collection performed at the health facility. Among the 93 women with prior screening experience who favored HPV testing, preference was evenly split between facility-based self-collection at 13.6 percent and provider-collected sampling at 13.9 percent. The study authors highlighted several operational considerations for health systems scaling up molecular testing within routine HIV services. Because existing clients exhibit strong loyalty to familiar VIAC protocols, programs must implement client-centered education that clarifies the clinical rationale and enhanced sensitivity of molecular HPV testing, as well as the safety of extended three-to-five-year screening intervals. Simultaneously, offering validated self-sampling options provides an actionable pathway to engage women who systematically avoid speculum examinations due to discomfort or modesty concerns, ensuring broader population coverage. Beyond core clinical history, the survey captured detailed social and demographic profiles across the three participating medical centers. Among all enrolled participants, 64.1 percent reported completing secondary education, and 66.3 percent were currently married. Religious affiliations were predominantly Christian at 44.3 percent, followed by Pentecostal at 24.4 percent and Apostolic at 19.7 percent. Facility representation included 164 women from Glenview Polyclinic, 163 from Tsholotsho District Hospital, and 124 from Guruve District Hospital. Among respondents with previous screening experience, 68.7 percent had undergone visual evaluation one to two years prior, 25.7 percent within the preceding twelve months, and 5.6 percent more than two years earlier. Study procedures adhered to protocols approved by the Medical Research Council of Zimbabwe and evaluated under United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention human research protection guidelines, with paper records digitized into CommCare and analyzed in R software. The investigation highlighted practical service delivery dynamics, particularly the physical and time burdens borne by clients. A substantial majority of respondents had existing employment commitments, traveled on foot, and required at least thirty minutes to arrive at health facilities. Although differentiated HIV service delivery models, such as multi-month dispensing of antiretroviral drugs and community clubs, reduce clinic transit burdens and preserve viral suppression, they concurrently diminish regular face-to-face contacts with clinic workers. In supported sites, healthcare staff currently utilize a manual, color-coded sticker mechanism on medical records to identify clients overdue for visual screening. However, this visual tracking approach risks missing women enrolled in multi-month dispensing who visit clinics infrequently. Consequently, investigators suggested implementing automated tracking and alert systems to reliably schedule molecular testing every three to five years while documenting screening declinations for personalized follow-up. Participant age patterns also underscored the necessity of sustained educational outreach across different life stages. First-time screening uptake and procedural refusals were both documented among women aged 41 to 49 years despite their prolonged retention in primary HIV care. Under updated national guidance, primary molecular testing is directed toward women living with HIV between the ages of 25 and 49 years. The researchers emphasized that older women must not be neglected during this transition, citing global guidance recommending at least one molecular test for unscreened women aged 50 to 65 years when clinical visualization of the cervix is limited. Additionally, cultural and community networks offer critical touchpoints for health communication. Because approximately one quarter of refusing participants belonged to the Apostolic faith, a tradition previously linked to spiritual healing preferences over clinical preventive care, tailored provider dialogue and collaborative outreach with faith leaders could help dispel reservations regarding cancer prevention. The authors noted several methodological considerations that temper the generalizability of their conclusions. The cross-sectional sample was drawn exclusively from three public facilities, meaning findings might not capture conditions across all healthcare environments in Zimbabwe. Additionally, because most participants learned about molecular screening solely through the introductory questionnaire script, their stated acceptance levels and collection preferences represent preliminary perspectives. Potential social desirability bias was managed by deploying interviewer nurses separate from clinical screening providers, though investigators could not calculate the median interval between antiretroviral treatment initiation and first screening because initiation dates were unrecorded. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content About Us Contact Us Advertising Subscribe Membership News & Views Ed’s Blog Soapbox Appointments Women to Watch Politics Local World Business Employers Entrepreneurs Tech Leadership Advice Profiles Leadership Awards Life Books Money Screen Health Womens Health News Climate Sport Events Podcasts × Search for: × News & Views Ed’s Blog Soapbox Appointments Politics Local World Business Employers Entrepreneurs Tech Leadership Advice Profiles Leadership Awards Life Books Money Screen Sport Agenda Sports Health Womens Health News Climate Events Podcasts About Us Contact Us Advertising Subscribe Membership Search for: Ed's Blog Australia’s goal of eliminating cervical cancer at risk with falling vaccination rates by Angela Priestley | 4 days ago Has Australia gotten complacent on cervical cancer? With HPV vaccination rates falling and screening lagging, our goal of becoming the first country to eliminate cervical cancer can no longer be assumed. Australia promised to be the first country to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035, something I’ve previously described as one of the more positive stories in women’s health. But that goal could be slipping away as HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccinations have fallen below 80 per cent for the first time, and to their lowest levels since the national program began in 2007. Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers that is almost entirely preventable. While an elimination goal once seemed like a dream, it is well within reach for Australia if we can maintain vaccination rates and cervical screening participation. But HPC coverage dropped to 77.1 per cent in 2025, and down to 69.6 per cent among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adolescents – down more than 15 points since 2020. Meanwhile, only three-quarters of eligible Australians are up to date with screening. The Cervical Cancer Elimination Progress report released today for World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day shows that the proportion of girls receiving a dose of HPV vaccine by age 15 fell from 80 per cent to 78.7 per cent, while coverage for boys also continued to decline, falling to 75.6 per cent The report notes that sustained vaccination coverage below 80 per cent is not sufficient for achieving elimination of the targeted HPV types in the longer term, and experts are calling for urgent action to reverse the trend. As Julia Brotherton (pictured above), lead author of the report, says, Australia’s made extraordinary progress in eliminating cancer, but this progress can’t be taken for granted. “Anyone aged 25 or under who has missed their HPV vaccination can catch up with a free single dose. I encourage young people and parents to speak with their GP, nurse or pharmacist,” says Brotherton, who is also Professor of Cancer Prevention at the University of Melbourne. Professor Lisa Whop, Associate Director of Research and Cervical Cancer Elimination Team Lead at Yardhura Walani, the Australian National University, also notes how quickly the hard-won gains can be lost, sharing concern for the decline in HPV vaccination among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adolescents. “We need sustained investment in culturally safe, community-led approaches, stronger partnerships with Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations and schools, and better pathways to reach young people who miss school-based vaccination,” she said. The vaccine protects against high-risk strains of HPV that lead to cancers of the cervix, vaina, vulva, penis, anus and back of the throat. It can also protect against non-cancer-causing HPV strains that are responsible for the vast majority of genital warts. The vaccine works best before a person is ever exposed through sexual contact, which is why it’s typically recommended it’s given to early adolescence. The World Health Organisation urged the globe to work together to eliminate cervical cancer in 2018, and it is an area of health that has shown that the eradication of a disease could be possible with leadership and sustained focus. The work that has been achieved – including moving recently to the availability of a self-collection method for screening, improving participation rates among under-screened populations – comes as a result of decades of support for an organised approach that is the cervical screening program. Australia’s National Strategy for the Elimination of Cervical Cancer was launched in November 2023, with the goal of elimination by 2035. Its modelling includes targets of 90 per cent vaccination coverage among eligible people, 70 per cent participation in five-yearly cervical screening, and 95 per cent of eligible people receiving optimal treatment for cervical precancer and cancer. But as Professor Marion Saville told me in 2021, equity in the program has always been the biggest challenge. Communities can’t be left behind in Australia’s race to be the first country to eliminate cervical cancer, especially Aboriginal women who are already two and a half to three times more likely to develop this cancer than other Australian women. Around 250 Australian women die from cervical cancer each year, according to Cancer Australia. Mortality rates dropped significantly in recent decades due to the immunisation and screening program, but the majority of individuals who do die of cervical cancer have either never participated in screening or are under-screened, according to the Australian Centre for Disease Control. All of this shows why cervical screening remains critical, even despite Australia’s successful HPV vaccination program – something I’ll admit I personally fell behind on until earlier this year, actually thinking the vaccination program had it sorted. So take this as a reminder to check if you’re overdue for screening, or to get that first vaccination dose for those 25 and under. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Bruceine D Induces Ferroptosis in Immortalized Ectocervical Epithelial Cells by November 19, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Bruceine D Induces Ferroptosis in Immortalized Ectocervical Epithelial Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A plant-derived compound called bruceine D significantly reduced the survival of human papillomavirus-immortalized cervical cells by triggering ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Researchers identified the quassinoid, isolated from Brucea javanica, as an active agent capable of impairing ectocervical cells expressing HPV16 E6 and E7 oncogenes in laboratory culture. Because persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus strains represents the primary underlying cause of cervical precancerous lesions and cervical cancer, evaluating compounds that trigger regulated cellular demise in affected tissues has become an area of active therapeutic investigation. To evaluate the biological effects of the natural compound, investigators conducted experiments on HPV16 E6/E7-immortalized ectocervical epithelial cells, designated as Ect1/E6E7. The team assessed cellular proliferation and health through multiple experimental assays, measuring cell viability, colony formation capacity, EdU incorporation, and cell-cycle progression. Across these assays, the treatment significantly inhibited cell proliferation and provoked cell-cycle arrest at the G0/G1 transition in a concentration-dependent manner, indicating that exposure prevented the cells from dividing normally. Subsequent laboratory tests demonstrated that the cellular death induced by bruceine D possessed the classical molecular hallmarks of ferroptosis. Following compound administration, the cervical cells showed a substantial increase in lipid peroxidation and elevated levels of malondialdehyde, a primary byproduct of lipid damage. In parallel, intracellular levels of the antioxidant glutathione were depleted, and mitochondrial function was severely disrupted, matching the metabolic imbalances typically observed when ferroptotic cascades are initiated. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Read Med Journals Study Anatomy Find Cancer Care The study also analyzed the expression of ferroptosis-related proteins to characterize the molecular cascades governed by the treatment. Exposure to bruceine D treatment downregulated GPX4 in the cultured cells. The functional contribution of this pathway was further validated through pharmacological rescue experiments, in which specific ferroptosis inhibitors partially reversed cell death, confirming that iron-dependent oxidative lethality contributed directly to the observed cytotoxicity. To uncover the regulatory networks acting alongside GPX4 downregulation, the researchers utilized network pharmacology analysis coupled with experimental validation. These integrated analyses implicated glutathione S-transferase P1, designated GSTP1, and mitogen-activated protein kinase 14, known as MAPK14, as central components in the cellular response to bruceine D. When the scientists applied pharmacological inhibitors targeting MAPK14, the ferroptotic responses were markedly attenuated, demonstrating that GSTP1 and MAPK14 signaling serves as an important regulatory pathway during compound exposure. Beyond single-agent administration, the researchers evaluated the impact of combining bruceine D with established small-molecule modulators of ferroptotic signaling. When administered alongside the known ferroptosis inducer erastin, the quassinoid exhibited synergistic antiproliferative effects, leading to an enhanced suppression of Ect1/E6E7 cell growth compared to individual treatments. The researchers noted that these preclinical findings warrant further experimental investigation into bruceine D and ferroptosis-targeted strategies in the context of HPV-associated cervical disease. to cervical cancer.On Tuesday, world cervical cancer elimination day, state health department published a government order approving ₹8.7 crore to screen 1.24 lakh women for high-risk HPV in five districts. The order, signed by health secretary Darez Ahamed, said the programme would be extended to other districts in phases, subject to Union government approval.The kits will allow women to take a vaginal swab themselves at their homes, without an intimate examination by a doctor or nurse. Health centres will collect the samples and send them to a laboratory. The programme will cover women aged 35 in Dharmapuri, Villupuram, Tiruvannamalai, Perambalur and Ariyalur. They will be screened again at 45, said Dr J Jayashree, programme officer for cancer care at the National Health Mission, Tamil Nadu.Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in Tamil Nadu, despite being largely preventable through vaccination, regular screening and timely treatment. The state’s cancer registry says it continues to rank second in the state and first in some districts, even as its incidence has declined. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like What She Discovered About Her Everyday Walking ShoesHF Stride Undo The new programme aims to identify women with high-risk HPV infections and treat precancerous changes before they develop into cancer. “Self-collection could help reach women who are reluctant to visit a hospital or undergo an examination,” she said. Officials are identifying a vendor to carry out the laboratory tests. The test looks for the genetic material of high-risk types of HPV virus. “It checks for the virus, not a woman’s inherited cancer risk. A positive result means she carries the virus,” she said.Until now, Tamil Nadu has largely screened for cervical cancer by having a health worker examine the cervix, the lower part of the womb, after applying dilute acetic acid. The worker looks for changes that may signal abnormal cells. That method depends on the examiner’s skill and judgement, Dr Jayashree said. The HPV test is more sensitive and less dependent on visual interpretation.Women who test positive will need further checks to determine whether the infection has caused abnormal cell changes. Those found to have precancerous changes — cells that could become cancer if left untreated — will receive treatment. Women diagnosed with cancer will be referred for cancer care. “Most HPV infections clear on their own. But an infection that persists can cause changes in cervical cells and, over time, lead to cancer. The vaccination drive protects girls against HPV, while screening helps identify women who need further assessment and treatment, she said. HPV 疫苗在全球已使用多年,经过包括世界卫生组织(WHO)在内的多家国际权威机构严格评估,安全性已得到充分验证;我国上市的HPV疫苗还经过国家药品监督管理部门每批次合格性检测,安全性能够得到保证。与其他常规疫苗一样,接种后可能出现局部红肿、疼痛,或一过性低热、乏力等,均属轻微的一般反应,通常1—3天内自行缓解,无需过度担心。 问题三:以前接种过HPV疫苗,还需要再接种吗? 不需要。对于16型和18型HPV引起的癌前病变和癌症,纳入免疫规划的双价疫苗的免疫原性和有效性与九价相当。既往已完成双价、四价、九价HPV疫苗任何全程接种者,无需重复接种。 本文来自大风号,仅代表大风号自媒体观点。 凤凰V现场 独家对话深蓝CEO姜海荣:大模型上车,车机正在告别“听指令” 德国IFA直击:中国企业如何用AI读懂一个家?2026中国联通合作伙伴大会在上海举行,九大成果看联通智能化布局华为Mate XT 2展翼三折叠深度体验:三折叠的新答案IFA 2026 ,安克硬控全场查看更多

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Six-Gene Panel Distinguishes HPV-Positive Cervical and Head and Neck Cancers by November 17, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Six-Gene Panel Distinguishes HPV-Positive Cervical and Head and Neck Cancers Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive investigation integrating bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses has identified 52 shared genes associated with human papillomavirus across cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. From this group of shared alterations, a machine learning-based feature selection strategy prioritised a six-gene panel consisting of CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, MCM2, KCNS1, EFNB3, and COL28A1. This prioritised panel consistently distinguished HPV-positive tumours from HPV-negative tumours in both malignancies, pointing to common molecular pathways driven by viral infection despite the different anatomical origins of the two cancers. Human papillomavirus is recognised as the primary cause of cervical cancer and is also an increasingly significant contributor to head and neck malignancies. Although cervical tumours and head and neck tumours emerge from distinct anatomical sites, their development shares an underlying viral aetiology. Despite this common causative factor, the molecular alterations associated with HPV across both disease types have remained incompletely understood, creating a need for comparative transcriptional studies to clarify the shared biological mechanisms underlying HPV-driven carcinogenesis. To detect transcriptional patterns common to both cancer types, the researchers designed an analytical framework combining differential expression analysis with weighted gene co-expression network analysis. They applied these computational techniques to compare HPV-positive tumours against normal tissues in both cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. This initial comparative step was structured to capture shared tumour-associated genes that deviate from baseline expression in healthy non-cancerous tissues across both sites. Discover more Find Cancer Care Cancers cancer cancers Cancer Because general tumour-related changes can overlap with virus-specific signatures, the research team implemented an additional filtering step to isolate alterations uniquely linked to human papillomavirus. The shared tumour-associated genes were refined by conducting direct comparisons between HPV-positive tumours and HPV-negative tumours within both cervical and head and neck cancer datasets. Candidate genes that emerged from this comparative refinement were subsequently processed through a machine learning-based feature selection strategy to identify the most robust predictive markers. The integrated differential expression and co-expression network pipeline initially yielded a total of 52 shared HPV-associated genes, from which the machine learning strategy prioritised six specific targets: CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, MCM2, KCNS1, EFNB3, and COL28A1. When evaluated across patient cohorts, this six-gene panel demonstrated a consistent ability to distinguish HPV-positive from HPV-negative tumours in both cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. Furthermore, the panel maintained similar expression patterns when tested against independent transcriptomic validation cohorts. To resolve how these candidate markers behave at cellular resolution, the authors examined single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from both tumour types. This analysis demonstrated that all six prioritised genes were predominantly expressed within epithelial cells. Within these epithelial cell populations, the directional expression changes corresponded to viral status: CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, KCNS1, and MCM2 showed increased expression levels in HPV-positive samples, whereas EFNB3 and COL28A1 exhibited reduced expression in the presence of HPV infection. Functional annotation indicated that the six prioritised genes participate in key biological processes directly relevant to tumour progression. These biological functions include cell-cycle regulation, DNA replication, extracellular matrix organisation, and cell-to-cell communication. In establishing the scientific rationale for the investigation, the authors noted that persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus represents the established, necessary cause of cervical cancer development, even though only a small proportion of HPV infections ultimately advance to high-grade cervical lesions or invasive malignancy. Clinical researchers have hypothesized that co-infections with genital mycoplasmas or classical sexually transmitted infections could potentially influence HPV persistence and disease progression, or alternatively impair the clinical accuracy of visual screening modalities by inducing local mucosal inflammation. Within Ethiopia, however, rigorous empirical evidence regarding the specific associations between these diverse sexually transmitted microbes, hrHPV infection status, histological cervical lesions, and visual inspection with acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine (VIA/VILI) has historically remained limited. To address this knowledge gap, the research team analyzed vaginal self-samples obtained from a study cohort of 885 Ethiopian women who participated in HPV-based cervical cancer screening protocols. The biological specimens were evaluated via real-time polymerase chain reaction (real-time PCR) assays designed to detect 14 high-risk HPV types, three classical sexually transmitted bacterial and protozoan pathogens—specifically Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis—and four species of genital mycoplasmas. Following initial molecular testing, clinical management pathways directed 156 women who tested positive for hrHPV to undergo visual inspection examinations using acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine, while 116 women subsequently underwent histological tissue examinations to establish definitive diagnostic classifications. Discover more Find Cancer Care See an OB-GYN Find Skin Care Book a Checkup Check Symptoms The authors employed rigorous analytical approaches to evaluate the collected epidemiological and molecular data, summarizing categorical variables through descriptive frequencies and percentages. Bivariate associations between the identified microbial detections and designated outcome variables were examined using chi-square tests alongside logistic regression models. The molecular analysis established that 568 participants, representing 64.2 percent of the study population (95 percent confidence interval: 61 to 67 percent), tested positive for at least one sexually transmitted microbe. Classical sexually transmitted infections were present in a relatively small subset of participants, yielding an overall prevalence of 4.3 percent (95 percent confidence interval: 3.1 to 5.8 percent). By contrast, genital mycoplasmas were widely distributed across the screening cohort, being identified in 64 percent of the women (95 percent confidence interval: 60.7 to 67.1 percent). Among the various mycoplasma species detected by real-time PCR, Ureaplasma parvum was documented as the most frequently identified organism, while approximately one out of every five women in the broader cohort was diagnosed with an hrHPV infection. Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that the detection of high-risk HPV was significantly associated with several distinct microbial detections and systemic infections. High-risk HPV positivity was statistically associated with the presence of genital mycoplasma detection (adjusted odds ratio = 1.7, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.3 to 2.3, p = 0.001), Chlamydia trachomatis infection (adjusted odds ratio = 5.4, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.4 to 21, p = 0.014), and Mycoplasma hominis detection (adjusted odds ratio = 2.0, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.4 to 3.0, p = 0.001). Furthermore, high-risk HPV was strongly associated with concurrent human immunodeficiency virus infection, which demonstrated an adjusted odds ratio of 3.2 (95 percent confidence interval: 1.8 to 5.5, p < 0.001). When evaluating tissue outcomes, histological examination revealed that cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) lesions were strongly associated with both high-risk HPV infection (adjusted odds ratio = 6.77, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.2 to 75.4, p = 0.03) and HIV infection (adjusted odds ratio = 8.92, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.5 to 72.2, p = 0.02). In contrast, neither the presence of classical sexually transmitted infections nor the detection of genital mycoplasmas showed a statistically significant association with CIN2+ cervical lesions or with the clinical outcomes of visual inspection using acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine. supplementary_news.content: Province adopts HPV testing as primary cervical cancer screening tool Officials say the test can detect high‐risk infections before abnormal cell changes occur, allowing for earlier intervention The provincial government is transitioning to the human papillomavirus (HPV) test from the Pap test as the main form of cervical cancer screening in hopes of progressing cervical cancer prevention. HPV testing can detect the virus responsible for cervical cancer before abnormal cellular changes. This allows for earlier identification of people at risk and supports timely follow-up and intervention. "The research is clear; early detection of cancer can help save lives. By transitioning to HPV testing, we are improving our ability to identify individuals at risk of cervical cancer earlier, which is essential for prevention," said Health Minister John Dornan. "This change ensures that New Brunswickers have access to the most accurate, efficient and effective screening available." The move aligns with international and federal efforts to eliminate cervical cancer, including Canada's 2040 elimination goal. The work is in collaboration with all provinces and territories, which are at various stages of transitioning to HPV testing. "Switching to HPV testing represents a vital step forward in the fight against cervical cancer," said Dr. Eshwar Kumar, medical officer at the New Brunswick Cancer Network. "This approach allows us to pinpoint high-risk individuals earlier and implement the preventative care needed to save lives, giving New Brunswickers the best chance for long-term health." Health officials encourage New Brunswickers to maintain routine screening through their primary care provider. HPV testing is recommended every five years for women, trans men and gender-diverse people aged 25 to 69 who have a cervix and have ever been sexually active. People should speak with their provider about their personal screening needs. "Preventing cancer before it starts is one of the most powerful ways to save lives," said Andrea Seale, CEO of the Canadian Cancer Society. "We applaud New Brunswick for making HPV testing its primary cervical cancer screening method. This reflects the kind of action needed to deliver on Canada's commitment, reaffirmed through the G7, to eliminate cervical cancer, and is meaningful progress for New Brunswickers." A positive HPV test doesn't mean someone has cervical cancer; additional testing or follow-up may be recommended, depending on the results. More information about accessing cervical cancer screening is available on the government's website. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Pap smear, medical screening procedure used to detect precancerous and cancerous changes in the cells of the cervix. Developed in the 1940s by physician George Papanicolaou, the test involves collecting cells from the cervical surface during a pelvic examination and then investigating them microscopically for abnormalities. A Pap smear typically entails the collection of two specimens for laboratory staining and examination, one consisting of vaginal secretions from the ectocervix and the other of scrapings from the surface of the endocervical canal, where cancerous growth frequently originates. In practice, these cells may be collected together in one sample, such as when using a broom-type device for liquid-based cytology, or they may be collected separately, such as with a spatula for the ectocervix and a brush for the endocervical canal, and then combined in a single specimen vial or slide. The Pap smear may reveal malignant cells not only from the cervix but also from the endometrium (the mucous coat of the uterus) and the ovaries. The development of other cervical cancer screening methods, particularly human papillomavirus (HPV) testing and liquid-based cytology, has reshaped the role of the Pap smear in clinical practice. HPV testing, which directly detects the virus responsible for most cervical cancers, is more sensitive than cytology alone and in many regions of the world has been adopted as a primary screening tool or in combination with Pap smears (co-testing). Liquid-based cytology, introduced in the 1990s, improved sample quality and allowed concurrent HPV testing from the same specimen, increasing diagnostic efficiency. As a result, Pap smears are now performed less frequently, often at longer intervals (every 3–5 years rather than annually or biennially), and in some regions they are being replaced altogether by HPV-based screening. Despite these changes, the Pap smear remains an important tool worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings where HPV testing may be less accessible, and continues to be credited with dramatically reducing cervical cancer incidence and mortality since its introduction. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Honeycomb Ultrasound Patterns May Signal HPV-Independent Cervical Adenocarcinoma in Case Series by November 15, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Honeycomb Ultrasound Patterns May Signal HPV-Independent Cervical Adenocarcinoma in Case Series Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a retrospective case series analyzing patients who underwent surgery between August 2017 and September 2024, researchers have documented the clinical presentation and preoperative imaging patterns associated with gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma. Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma, commonly designated as G-EAC, is recognized as a distinct human papillomavirus-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma. To address these ongoing diagnostic difficulties, investigators reviewed records from thirteen patients with histopathologically confirmed disease at their medical center to characterize key clinical and sonographic manifestations and establish hypothesis-generating observations for subsequent clinical research. The investigated patient cohort consisted of thirteen parous women ranging from 39 to 76 years of age, with an overall mean age of 53.4 years across the series. An evaluation of presenting symptoms revealed that vaginal discharge was the most frequent complaint leading to evaluation, documented in eight of the thirteen patients, representing 61.5 percent of the cases. Irregular vaginal bleeding was identified as the second most common presenting symptom, reported in four of the thirteen women, or 30.8 percent. One patient, accounting for 7.7 percent of the cohort, presented with postcoital bleeding. Standard preoperative screening techniques demonstrated low diagnostic yields among the evaluated patients, underscoring the diagnostic hurdles typical of this human papillomavirus-independent malignancy. High-risk human papillomavirus testing returned negative findings in eleven of the thirteen individuals, or 84.6 percent. Cytological evaluation through ThinPrep cytologic testing, or TCT, similarly failed to identify malignant changes in the vast majority of cases, returning completely negative results in twelve of the thirteen women, or 92.3 percent. Discover more Find Cancer Care Donate to Research Read Med Journals Find Conferences Find an OBGYN Diagnostic limitations persisted when patients underwent colposcopic examination and directed tissue sampling prior to definitive surgical intervention. Among the eleven individuals in the cohort who underwent colposcopy accompanied by cervical biopsy, histopathological examination yielded negative results in eight of the eleven patients, or 72.7 percent. In two of the eleven biopsied individuals, representing 18.2 percent, the histopathological analysis identified mild glandular atypia. Definite neoplastic evidence was exceedingly rare during initial biopsy sampling, with rare adenocarcinoma cells identified in only one of the eleven patients, representing 9.1 percent of those who underwent the procedure. Ultrasound assessments raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in nine of the thirteen patients, or 69.2 percent. In contrast, sonographic findings were interpreted as suggestive of benign cervical cystic lesions in two of the thirteen patients, representing 15.4 percent, while findings were considered unremarkable in the remaining two patients, also accounting for 15.4 percent. Specific sonographic features were frequently observed across the cohort, including a characteristic honeycomb sonographic pattern identified in seven of the thirteen patients, or 53.8 percent. In addition, marked intralesional blood flow designated as Adler grade III abundant vascularity was detected in nine of the thirteen patients, representing 69.2 percent of the evaluated group. The study authors, affiliated with the Hunan Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital in Changsha, China, concluded that gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma may come to clinical attention through a combination of presenting symptoms and sonographic findings that collectively raise diagnostic suspicion. The researchers emphasized, however, that these findings remain strictly descriptive observations derived from a single-center retrospective series of thirteen patients, highlighting that larger, adequately controlled clinical studies are required to validate the diagnostic utility of these sonographic and clinical characteristics. 收藏 微博 分享 MD 微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 (来源:德馨顺城) 宫颈癌,是严重威胁全球女性生命健康的恶性肿瘤,也是目前人类唯一可以通过疫苗预防的癌症。大量医学研究证实,几乎所有宫颈癌的发生,都与高危型人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)的持续感染密切相关。而接种HPV疫苗,是预防HPV感染、阻断宫颈癌发病链条,最经济、高效、科学的核心手段,是守护女性一生生殖健康的第一道坚固防线。 读懂HPV:无处不在的健康隐患 HPV病毒是一种极为常见的生殖道病毒,传播途径广泛,主要通过密切接触传播,有性生活的人群一生中感染HPV的概率高达80%以上。多数人感染后可自行清除病毒,但少数人会出现持续高危型感染,长期刺激宫颈细胞,逐步引发病变,最终发展为宫颈癌。 我国女性HPV感染存在两个高峰阶段,分别为17-24岁青年时期和40-44岁中年时期,覆盖女性青春、育龄、中年等关键人生阶段,隐蔽性强、危害持久。宫颈癌发病不可逆,且逐年呈现年轻化趋势,提前预防、主动防护,远比后期治疗更为重要。 黄金接种期:越早接种,保护力越强 世界卫生组织(WHO)明确推荐:9-14岁是接种HPV疫苗的黄金年龄。 这个阶段的青少年女孩,免疫系统发育完善,在尚未暴露于HPV病毒风险前接种,身体可产生远超成年人的抗体水平,抗体浓度是15岁以上人群的2倍以上,且保护时效更长久、防护效果更稳定,能最大程度规避后续病毒感染风险,实现最优预防效果。 很多人存在误区,认为“年纪小无需接种”“没有症状不用预防”。实则恰恰相反,HPV预防的核心关键,就是在病毒感染前建立免疫屏障。越早完成接种,越早获得专属保护,为终身生殖健康保驾护航。 多款疫苗适配全人群,按需选择无需焦虑 目前国内正规上市的HPV疫苗,分为二价、四价、九价三类,价数代表可预防的HPV病毒亚型种类,适配不同年龄、不同需求的女性,覆盖全面、各有优势。目前,我市主要有二价和九价2类HPV疫苗: 1.二价HPV疫苗:核心防护16、18型两种最高危病毒,这两种亚型诱发了全球70%以上的宫颈癌。适配9-45岁女性,性价比高、货源充足,是基础预防的优选,目前已纳入国家免疫规划。 2.九价HPV疫苗:覆盖9种高危及低危HPV亚型,可预防90%以上的宫颈癌及相关生殖道疾病,防护范围最广,适配9-45岁人群。 国家惠民政策落地,守护青少年健康 为全面降低我国女性宫颈癌发病率,国家已正式将13周岁适龄女孩免费接种二价HPV疫苗纳入国家免疫规划。 免费接种核心政策 •接种人群:2011年11月10日后出生、年满13周岁的适龄女孩 •接种剂次:全程2剂次,两剂间隔6个月,最长不超过1年 •接种地点:社区卫生服务中心、乡镇卫生院 这项普惠民生的健康政策,为青少年女孩免费搭建健康屏障,从源头降低下一代宫颈癌发病风险,是国家送给适龄女孩最珍贵的“健康礼”。免疫规划既是公民权利,也是公民义务,监护人应依法保证适龄儿童按时接种免疫规划疫苗。 破除常见误区,科学理性接种 1.误区1:接种疫苗就不会得宫颈癌 真相:HPV疫苗可预防绝大多数宫颈癌,但无法覆盖所有致病亚型,也不能替代日常筛查。疫苗接种+定期宫颈筛查,才是完整的防癌保障。 2.误区2:已有性生活、年纪大就不用接种 真相:无论是否有性生活、是否已婚、年龄大小,只要在接种年龄段,未感染对应高危亚型病毒,接种后均可获得有效保护,大龄女性依然有接种价值。 3.误区3:HPV疫苗只保护女性 真相:HPV病毒同样会引发男性尖锐湿疣、肛门癌等疾病,男性接种也可实现自我防护,同时减少病毒交叉传播,守护家人健康。 为爱接种,守护无恙 健康,是人生最珍贵的底色,也是陪伴一生的财富。宫颈癌可防可控,无需谈“癌”色变,主动接种HPV疫苗、定期做好健康筛查、树立健康防护意识,就能有效规避疾病风险。 无论是正值青春的少女,还是守护家庭的女性,都请重视生殖健康,把握黄金接种时机。积极接种HPV疫苗,主动筑牢免疫屏障,远离疾病困扰,拥抱自在健康人生! 温馨提示:所有HPV疫苗请通过正规接种单位接种,杜绝非正规渠道,保障接种安全。 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP 新浪财经声明:此消息系转载自合作媒体,新浪财经登载此文出于传递更多信息之目的,文章内容仅供参考,不构成投资建议。
